pos: n. pl. (cataracts or torrents of falling water; the noise under which the psalmist is overwhelmed)
etymology: A compound of water and spout, from Middle Dutch spuiten, to gush. It renders Hebrew tsinnor, a pipe, conduit or waterfall — used elsewhere of the gutter by which Joab entered Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me. The psalmist is in exile from the sanctuary, cast down and disquieted, remembering God from the land of Jordan and the Hermonites — the headwaters, where the snowmelt comes off the mountain in cataracts. He hears the roar of falling water and hears his own life in it: one depth calling to another, wave after wave, nothing between them. Two things in the verse are easy to miss. The first is the possessive: thy waterspouts, thy waves, thy billows. He does not describe his troubles as accidents or as the work of enemies but as God's own water going over him. The second is the refrain that frames it on both sides — Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him. The man is preaching to himself in the middle of the noise, and the sermon is a command and a future tense. Jonah, in the belly of the fish, uses almost the same words: thou hadst cast me into the deep, all thy billows and thy waves passed over me. Both men knew whose water it was, and both were heard.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a spout or gush of water; in the older sense, a cataract or fall of water from on high.
webster_full: WATERSPOUT, n. A remarkable meteor, consisting of a cloud in the form of a cone, from which a column of water descends.
SPOUT, n. A pipe or a projecting mouth of a vessel, useful in directing the stream of a liquid.
BILLOW, n. A great wave or surge of the sea, occasioned usually by violent wind.
CATARACT, n. A great fall of water over a precipice.
DISQUIET, v.t. To disturb; to deprive of peace, rest or tranquillity; to make uneasy or restless.
scriptures: Psalm 42:7
Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me.
Psalm 42:6
O my God, my soul is cast down within me: therefore will I remember thee from the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites, from the hill Mizar.
Psalm 42:5
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance.
Jonah 2:3
For thou hadst cast me into the deep, in the midst of the seas; and the floods compassed me about: all thy billows and thy waves passed over me.
corruption_summary: Spiritual darkness is handled as a chemical problem or as a failure of faith; Psalm 42 gives a believer overwhelmed, naming the water as God's, and preaching to his own soul in the middle of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Two bad counsels meet over a man in Psalm 42's condition. The first treats the darkness as purely a defect of body or brain, a matter to be managed and nothing more; the second treats it as proof of unbelief, to be repented of. Scripture does neither. It gives the sufferer words — a whole psalm of them — and lets him say that his tears have been his meat day and night, that his soul is cast down, that deep calls to deep. It does not hurry him. Elijah under the juniper tree was given sleep and food before he was given a word, and the word, when it came, was not a rebuke.

But the psalm does not leave him lying there either. Three times it turns and addresses the man himself: Why art thou cast down, O my soul?... hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him. That is a believer taking himself in hand, arguing with his own feelings from what he knows, and refusing to let the loudest voice in the room be the water. The cure is not a mood he manufactures; it is a hope fixed on someone outside him, stated in the future tense — I shall yet praise him — and held while the billows are still going over.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsinnor (H6794), a conduit or waterfall; tehom (H8415), the deep; mishbar (H4867), a breaker or wave; gal (H1530), a billow.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsinnor (H6794) — a pipe or cataract; used only here and of the gutter at the taking of Jerusalem.
Hebrew tehom (H8415) — the deep; the same word as the deep upon whose face darkness lay in Genesis 1.
Hebrew mishbar (H4867) — a breaker; rendered waves, and used again by Jonah.
Hebrew gal (H1530) — a billow, a heap; the second of the two words rolling over the psalmist.
Hebrew yachal (H3176) — to wait, to hope; the command the psalmist gives his own soul.
usage: “Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts” — trouble heard as one wave summoning the next.
“all thy waves and thy billows” — the possessive that changes the whole psalm.
“hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him” — a man preaching to himself.

pos: n. (an inundation; the rising water the psalmist prays will not close over him)
etymology: A compound of water and flood, Old English flod, from the root of flow. It renders Hebrew shibboleth in the sense of a flowing stream — the same word whose pronunciation betrayed the Ephraimites at the fords of Jordan.
biblical_def: Let not the waterflood overflow me, neither let the deep swallow me up, and let not the pit shut her mouth upon me. Three images of being closed in, rising in severity: water over the head, the deep swallowing, and finally the pit shutting its mouth like a living thing. Psalm 69 is the psalm of a man sinking — I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me — and it is quoted in the New Testament more than almost any other, always of Christ: the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; they gave me vinegar to drink; they hated me without a cause. The waterflood is therefore not only David's trouble but a description of what the Lord went into on behalf of his people. Two other verses stand over this one and govern it. Psalm 32 promises that in the floods of great waters they shall not come nigh unto the godly man. And Psalm 29, after seven verses of thunder and shattered cedars, says the thing that settles the matter: The LORD sitteth upon the flood; yea, the LORD sitteth King for ever. The water rises; it does not rise above the throne.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a flood of water; an inundation; a body of water rising and overflowing the low grounds.
webster_full: WATERFLOOD, n. A flood of water; an inundation.
FLOOD, n. A great flow of water; a body of moving water; an inundation; a deluge.
OVERFLOW, v.t. To spread over, as water; to inundate; to cover with water.
PIT, n. An artificial cavity made in the earth; a deep place; the grave.
INUNDATION, n. An overflow of water or other fluid; a flood; a rising and spreading of water over low grounds.
scriptures: Psalm 69:15
Let not the waterflood overflow me, neither let the deep swallow me up, and let not the pit shut her mouth upon me.
Psalm 69:2
I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me.
Psalm 32:6
For this shall every one that is godly pray unto thee in a time when thou mayest be found: surely in the floods of great waters they shall not come nigh unto him.
Psalm 29:10
The LORD sitteth upon the flood; yea, the LORD sitteth King for ever.
corruption_summary: Prayer in distress is recast as a technique for managing one's own state; the psalmist asks God to do something specific, names the danger plainly, and grounds the request in God's throne rather than in his own composure.
corruption_paragraphs: Prayer is widely taught now as a practice that works on the one praying — a way of centring, processing, becoming present. Psalm 69 has no interest in that. It is a petition addressed to someone who can act: let not the waterflood overflow me. The psalmist is not reframing his experience; he is asking to be pulled out of it, and he is specific about what he fears. Scripture is full of this plainness — deliver me, hear me, save me, make haste to help me — and a prayer life that has lost the imperative has usually lost the person it was addressed to as well.

The psalm also refuses the opposite error, which is to pray as if the outcome were in doubt because God's power were in doubt. Psalm 29 has just finished describing a storm that breaks the cedars of Lebanon and shakes the wilderness, and its conclusion is not that the storm is terrible but that the LORD sitteth upon the flood. The same water that goes over a man's head is under the feet of God's throne. That is why the godly may pray in the time when he may be found and be confident that the floods of great waters shall not come nigh him — not because the water stops rising, but because of who is sitting above it.
roots_summary: Hebrew shibboleth (H7641), a flowing stream; mabbul (H3999), the flood; metsulah (H4688), the deep; beer (H875), a pit or well.
roots_lines: Hebrew shibboleth (H7641) — a flowing stream; rendered waterflood, and famous from the fords of Jordan.
Hebrew mabbul (H3999) — the flood; used of Noah's deluge, and in Psalm 29 of the throne above it.
Hebrew metsulah (H4688) — a depth; neither let the deep swallow me up.
Hebrew beer (H875) — a pit or cistern; the mouth that shuts in the third image.
Hebrew yaven (H3121) — mire; I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing.
usage: “Let not the waterflood overflow me” — a petition, not a meditation.
“where there is no standing” — the exact nature of the danger named.
“The LORD sitteth upon the flood” — the answer above the water.

pos: n. pl. (channels with gates for controlling water; part of Egypt's doomed irrigation economy)
etymology: From Old French escluse, from Late Latin exclusa, a floodgate — literally something shut out. In Isaiah it stands in a phrase describing those who make ponds and channels for fish, the artificial waterworks of the Nile delta.
biblical_def: Isaiah 19 is a burden against Egypt, and its most devastating stroke is not military. The waters shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up. Egypt was the Nile; everything the country had — the flax, the fish, the fowling, the reeds, the annual flood that made the fields — came from one river that had never failed. Isaiah says it will. Then he walks through the economy trade by trade. The fishers shall mourn, and all they that cast angle into the brooks shall lament, and they that spread nets upon the waters shall languish; and they shall be broken in the purposes thereof, all that make sluices and ponds for fish. The sluice-makers are the engineers, the men whose skill had domesticated the river with gates and channels and stocked ponds. Their purposes break, because the thing they were managing is gone. Egypt is Scripture's standing picture of a civilization that trusts what it can see and control, and Israel's standing temptation was to lean on it: woe to them that go down to Egypt for help, and stay on horses, and trust in chariots. The sluices were real engineering and they were excellent, and they could not make it rain.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the stream of water issuing through a floodgate; a vent for water; an opening or channel with a gate.
webster_full: SLUICE, n. The stream of water issuing through a floodgate; or the floodgate itself; a vent for water.
SLUICE, v.t. To emit by flood gates; to wet abundantly.
POND, n. A body of stagnant water without an outlet, larger than a puddle, and smaller than a lake.
CHANNEL, n. The hollow bed of running waters; a canal or artificial cut for water.
PURPOSE, n. That which a person sets before himself as an object to be reached or accomplished; design; intention.
scriptures: Isaiah 19:10
And they shall be broken in the purposes thereof, all that make sluices and ponds for fish.
Isaiah 19:5
And the waters shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up.
Isaiah 19:8
The fishers also shall mourn, and all they that cast angle into the brooks shall lament, and they that spread nets upon the waters shall languish.
Ecclesiastes 2:6
I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees:
corruption_summary: Technical mastery is taken as security — a system engineered well enough is thought beyond failure; Isaiah breaks the sluice-makers' purposes by drying the river their whole craft presupposed.
corruption_paragraphs: Egypt's engineers were not fools and Isaiah does not call them fools. Their sluices worked. What the prophecy exposes is the hidden assumption underneath every such system: that the supply will continue. Modern equivalents are easy to name and painful to examine — supply chains, grids, credit, the assumption that food appears in shops. Scripture's quarrel is not with skill or with planning; Joseph stored grain for seven years by the wisdom of God, and Proverbs praises the ant that provideth her meat in the summer. It is with the confidence that competent arrangements have removed our dependence on God, when in fact they have only made it harder to notice.

Solomon ran the experiment from the inside and wrote it down. I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees — along with houses, vineyards, gardens, orchards, servants, silver and gold, and every delight he could name. His verdict on the whole works was vanity and vexation of spirit. Not because the pools were wrong, but because they could not do what he had half-hoped they would. The remedy is not to build worse but to hold what we build the way James instructs: ye ought to say, if the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.
roots_summary: Hebrew seker (H7938), a dam or enclosure of water; yeor (H2975), the Nile; agam (H98), a pool or marsh; charash (H2796), a craftsman.
roots_lines: Hebrew seker (H7938) — a dammed enclosure; rendered sluices, used once in Scripture.
Hebrew yeor (H2975) — the Nile, the river; the whole subject of Isaiah's burden against Egypt.
Hebrew agam (H98) — a pool or reedy marsh; the ponds for fish.
Hebrew amal (H535) — to languish, to be feeble; the fate of the fishermen and the flax workers alike.
Hebrew hevel (H1892) — vapour, vanity; Solomon's verdict on his own pools and orchards.
usage: “they shall be broken in the purposes thereof” — the engineers' plans, not their skill, undone.
“the river shall be wasted and dried up” — the assumption beneath the whole craft removed.
“I made me pools of water” — Solomon running the experiment and recording the verdict.

pos: n. pl. (ground poisoned with salt so that nothing grows; the sentence on Moab and Ammon)
etymology: A compound of salt and pit. In Zephaniah it renders Hebrew mikreh melach, a pit or quarry of salt — the salt flats around the Dead Sea, ground permanently barren.
biblical_def: Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, even the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation. The threat is geographical and the geography was in view: Moab and Ammon lay beside the Dead Sea, and everyone could see what the overthrow of Sodom had left. Moses had described it — the whole land thereof is brimstone, and salt, and burning, that it is not sown, nor beareth, nor any grass groweth therein. Salted ground is the most final judgment in the ancient world, because it does not merely destroy what stands; it ends the possibility of anything standing there again. Abimelech understood this when he took Shechem, slew its people, beat down the city, and sowed it with salt. And Lot's wife, looking back toward the cities, became a pillar of it. Yet salt is not simply a curse word in Scripture. Every meat offering was to be seasoned with it, and the covenant of God is called a covenant of salt. Christ tells his disciples ye are the salt of the earth, and warns that salt which has lost its savour is good for nothing. The same substance preserves a sacrifice and sterilizes a plain. What it does depends entirely on where God has put it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a pit where salt is obtained or formed; ground impregnated with salt and therefore barren.
webster_full: SALT-PIT, n. A pit where salt is obtained or made.
SALT, n. Common salt is the muriate of soda, used to season and preserve food.
BARREN, a. Not producing young, or offspring; unfruitful; not producing vegetation or plants.
DESOLATION, n. A place deserted or laid waste; destruction of inhabitants; gloominess.
NETTLE, n. A plant of the genus Urtica, whose prickles fret the skin and cause pain.
scriptures: Zephaniah 2:9

Therefore as I live, saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, even the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation: the residue of my people shall spoil them, and the remnant of my people shall possess them.
Deuteronomy 29:23

And that the whole land thereof is brimstone, and salt, and burning, that it is not sown, nor beareth, nor any grass groweth therein, like the overthrow of Sodom, and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger, and in his wrath:
Judges 9:45
And Abimelech fought against the city all that day; and he took the city, and slew the people that was therein, and beat down the city, and sowed it with salt.
Genesis 19:26
But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.
corruption_summary: Final judgment is dismissed as incompatible with a loving God; Scripture points at a salt plain that could be visited, and in the same breath names a remnant that would possess the land.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of a judgment that does not end is the hardest thing the Bible says, and the modern church has largely stopped saying it. What makes Zephaniah's threat so difficult to soften is that it points at evidence. The overthrow of Sodom was not a parable; Moses says the land is brimstone and salt and burning, and Zephaniah tells Moab to go and look at it. Christ, who spoke more about hell than anyone else in Scripture, used the same method — he pointed at the valley of Hinnom where the fires burned, and said the worm dieth not. The doctrine is not the invention of harsh preachers. It is the plain speech of the gentlest man who ever lived.

But Zephaniah 2:9 does not end at the saltpits, and the second half is as much a part of the verse as the first: the residue of my people shall spoil them, and the remnant of my people shall possess them. There is always a remnant. The same short book that pronounces perpetual desolation on Moab ends with the LORD rejoicing over his people with singing and resting in his love. And Ruth, who came out of Moab, is in the line of David and of Christ. Judgment in Scripture is real, specific and final; it has never once been the whole of what God said.
roots_summary: Hebrew melach (H4417), salt; mikreh (H4379), a pit or quarry; charul (H2738), nettles; shemamah (H8077), desolation.
roots_lines: Hebrew melach (H4417) — salt; used of the covenant of salt, the meat offering, and the sterilized plain.
Hebrew mikreh (H4379) — a pit or quarry; the saltpits of Zephaniah's sentence.
Hebrew charul (H2738) — nettles; what grows where nothing useful will.
Hebrew shemamah (H8077) — a waste, a desolation; the standing word for judged land.
Hebrew sheerith (H7611) — a remnant, a residue; the other half of the same verse.
usage: “the breeding of nettles, and saltpits” — ground that will not grow anything again.
“sowed it with salt” — Abimelech making a city permanently uninhabitable.
“the remnant of my people shall possess them” — the promise in the same sentence.

pos: n. pl. (stocked pools of still water; the figure for the bride's eyes in the Song)
etymology: A compound of fish and pool, Old English pol. In the Song it renders Hebrew berekah, a reservoir or pool — the same word used of the pool of Gibeon and the pool of Siloam.
biblical_def: Thine eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bathrabbim. The comparison seems odd until one has stood by a reservoir at evening. Heshbon was a Moabite city in the high tableland, and its pools were the still water of a dry country — deep, clear, quiet, gathered where everything around was thirsty, and holding the sky. To say a woman's eyes are like them is to say they are deep and calm and full of light, and that a man could look into them a long while. The Song is a poem of married love, and the church has read it for two thousand years both as that and as a figure of Christ and his people, which is no accident in a Bible that calls the church a bride and the Lord a bridegroom. Pools elsewhere in Scripture are civic infrastructure and the mark of a prudent city — Hezekiah gathered the waters of the lower pool when Assyria came, and Solomon made him pools of water to water the wood. Here the engineering vocabulary is bent to a lover's use. Scripture is not embarrassed by beauty, and has no rule against a husband saying so at length.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a pool where fish are kept or bred; a small collection of standing water.
webster_full: FISHPOOL, n. A pool in which fishes are kept.
POOL, n. A small collection of water in a hollow place, supplied by a spring or rain.
RESERVOIR, n. A place where anything is kept in store, particularly a place where water is collected and kept.
COUNTENANCE, n. The whole form of the face, or system of features; the face; look; aspect.
COMELY, a. Handsome; graceful; having a pleasing appearance.
scriptures: Song of Solomon 7:4
Thy neck is as a tower of ivory; thine eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bathrabbim: thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus.
Ecclesiastes 2:6
I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees:
Isaiah 22:9
Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many: and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool.
Psalm 42:7
Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me.
corruption_summary: Married desire is treated either as the whole of love or as something the devout should be quiet about; the Song is a book of Scripture in which a husband and wife praise each other's bodies at length and God did not edit it out.
corruption_paragraphs: A certain strain of piety has always been uneasy with the Song, and has managed the discomfort by allegorizing every line until no bride is left in it. The church fathers found Christ in the fishpools and the tower of ivory, and much of what they saw is genuinely there — Scripture does make marriage a figure of Christ and the church, and Paul says so explicitly of Genesis 2. But the figure only works because the thing figured is real and good. God gave a book to his people in which a husband looks at his wife and describes her at length, and the existence of that book is itself a doctrine.

The age's error is the opposite and louder: desire detached from covenant, made its own justification, and then found to be thin. The Song will not be used that way either. Three times it charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up nor awake love until it please, and it ends by calling love strong as death, jealousy cruel as the grave, a flame with a most vehement flame — and immediately adds that if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned. It cannot be bought and it will not be hurried. Those are covenant words, spoken over fishpools and towers of ivory.
roots_summary: Hebrew berekah (H1295), a pool or reservoir; Cheshbon (H2809), Heshbon; ayin (H5869), an eye or a spring; ahavah (H160), love.
roots_lines: Hebrew berekah (H1295) — a pool; the word for Gibeon's pool and Bethesda's counterpart.
Hebrew Cheshbon (H2809) — Heshbon, a city of the Moabite tableland taken by Israel under Moses.
Hebrew ayin (H5869) — an eye, and also a spring of water; the same word does both, which the image exploits.
Hebrew ahavah (H160) — love; love is strong as death.
Hebrew shalhebethyah (H7957) — a most vehement flame, a flame of the LORD; the Song's last word on the subject.
usage: “thine eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon” — still water in a dry country.
“the waters of the lower pool” — the same vocabulary used for a city's defence.
“I made me pools of water” — the engineering sense, in Solomon's own words.

pos: n. pl. (a shade tree named among the groves of Israel's idolatry)
etymology: Old English elm, from Latin ulmus. In Hosea it renders Hebrew elah, a terebinth or strong tree — elsewhere translated oak or teil tree; the KJV varies the English because the Hebrew names a class of large shade trees rather than one species.
biblical_def: They sacrifice upon the tops of the mountains, and burn incense upon the hills, under oaks and poplars and elms, because the shadow thereof is good. Hosea is describing the high places, and the detail he chooses is the comfort of the shade. The trees were pleasant; that is why the worship was held there. Israel's idolatry did not feel like apostasy from the inside — it felt like a good day on a hill under a broad tree, with incense, in a place their fathers had used. That is precisely what made it so hard to root out, and why the law had ordered the groves destroyed before the people ever entered: ye shall utterly destroy all the places, wherein the nations which ye shall possess served their gods, upon the high mountains, and upon the hills, and under every green tree. Isaiah tells the same people they shall be ashamed of the oaks which ye have desired, and describes them enflaming themselves with idols under every green tree and slaying their children in the valleys. The sentence Hosea passes is exact and terrible — therefore your daughters shall commit whoredom. What the fathers did comfortably under a good shadow, the daughters paid for. False worship is never contained to the generation that finds it pleasant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a tree of the genus Ulmus, valued for its shade and timber; in Scripture, a large spreading tree of the groves.
webster_full: ELM, n. A tree of the genus Ulmus, much valued for its shade and for the beauty of its form.
GROVE, n. A cluster of trees of no great extent; in Scripture, a wood or cluster of trees consecrated to idol worship.
HIGH-PLACE, n. In Scripture, an eminence used for the worship of idols or for sacrifice.
SHADOW, n. Shade within defined limits; obscurity or deprivation of light.
INCENSE, n. Perfume exhaled by fire; the odors of spices and gums, burnt in religious rites.
scriptures: Hosea 4:13

They sacrifice upon the tops of the mountains, and burn incense upon the hills, under oaks and poplars and elms, because the shadow thereof is good: therefore your daughters shall commit whoredom, and your spouses shall commit adultery.
Deuteronomy 12:2
Ye shall utterly destroy all the places, wherein the nations which ye shall possess served their gods, upon the high mountains, and upon the hills, and under every green tree:
Isaiah 1:29
For they shall be ashamed of the oaks which ye have desired, and ye shall be confounded for the gardens that ye have chosen.
Isaiah 57:5
Enflaming yourselves with idols under every green tree, slaying the children in the valleys under the clifts of the rocks?
corruption_summary: Worship is evaluated by how it feels — the shadow being good — rather than by whether God commanded it; Hosea names the pleasantness as the very thing that kept Israel in the groves.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the pleasantness of a religious setting proves nothing about whether God is in it. Because the shadow thereof is good is Hosea's explanation for a whole nation's false worship, and it is an explanation, not an excuse. The question Scripture puts to any act of worship is the one put at Sinai and repeated by Christ against the traditions of the elders: who required this at your hand? In vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.

The second half of Hosea's verse is the part that should sober any father. Therefore your daughters shall commit whoredom, and your spouses shall commit adultery. The men are in view throughout the passage; the consequence lands on the household. God says two verses later, I will not punish your daughters when they commit whoredom, for themselves are separated with whores. A generation that worships comfortably in a place God never appointed does not pay the whole bill itself. What is treated as a harmless preference in a father becomes a settled practice in a child.
roots_summary: Hebrew elah (H424), a terebinth or strong tree; allon (H437), an oak; libneh (H3839), the poplar; bamah (H1116), a high place.
roots_lines: Hebrew elah (H424) — a terebinth; rendered elm here and oak or teil tree elsewhere.
Hebrew allon (H437) — an oak; the first tree in Hosea's list.
Hebrew libneh (H3839) — the poplar or white tree; the second, and the rods Jacob peeled.
Hebrew bamah (H1116) — a high place; the standing word for the hilltop shrines Judah's good kings kept failing to remove.
Hebrew asherah (H842) — a grove or wooden idol; what Deuteronomy commanded to be cut down.
usage: “under oaks and poplars and elms” — the furniture of the high places.
“because the shadow thereof is good” — the reason given, and the whole problem.
“ye shall be ashamed of the oaks which ye have desired” — Isaiah on the end of it.

pos: n. (a tree whose peeled rods Jacob set in the watering troughs)
etymology: Old English haesel, a hazel tree. In Genesis it renders Hebrew luz, generally taken to be the almond — the same word that names the city Luz, which Jacob himself renamed Bethel.
biblical_def: And Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods. He set the peeled rods in the watering troughs where the flocks came to drink and conceive, and the cattle brought forth ringstraked, speckled and spotted — which happened to be exactly the animals Laban had agreed would be Jacob's wages. The passage is often read as folk science, and as science it is nonsense; peeled sticks do not determine the markings of lambs. But Genesis is not endorsing the method, and Jacob himself, in the next chapter, gives a completely different account of what happened. He tells his wives that the angel of God spoke to him in a dream and said, Lift up now thine eyes, and see, all the rams which leap upon the cattle are ringstraked, speckled, and grisled: for I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee. God did it, and told him so, and the reason was Laban's twenty years of fraud. The rods were Jacob being Jacob — still contriving, still managing outcomes — while God was quietly doing the thing his scheme took credit for. The hazel is a small witness to a large pattern in his life.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a tree or shrub of the genus Corylus, bearing a nut; the wood of this tree.
webster_full: HAZEL, n. A tree or shrub of the genus Corylus, bearing a nut of an oval shape.
ROD, n. The shoot or long twig of any woody plant; a branch or the stem of a shrub.
PILL, v.t. To peel; to strip off bark or skin.
STRAKE, n. A streak; a stripe or line of color different from the ground.
RINGSTRAKED, a. Having circular streaks or lines on the body.
scriptures: Genesis 30:37
And Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods.
Genesis 30:38
And he set the rods which he had pilled before the flocks in the gutters in the watering troughs when the flocks came to drink, that they should conceive when they came to drink.
Genesis 31:12
And he said, Lift up now thine eyes, and see, all the rams which leap upon the cattle are ringstraked, speckled, and grisled: for I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee.
Genesis 25:26
And after that came his brother out, and his hand took hold on Esau's heel; and his name was called Jacob: and Isaac was threescore years old when she bare them.
corruption_summary: Scripture is charged with teaching bad biology here, or else the rods are defended as though they worked; Genesis records what Jacob did and then lets God explain, two chapters later, what actually happened.
corruption_paragraphs: The passage is a favourite of critics, who read it as the Bible endorsing a superstition about prenatal influence. The charge misreads how Genesis narrates. Scripture constantly records what men did without approving it — Abraham's lie about Sarah, Jacob's deception of Isaac, David's census — and here it records a scheme and then supplies the true cause from the mouth of God: I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee. The flocks bred as they did because God intervened on behalf of a defrauded man, and the angel said so plainly in a dream. Jacob's rods are in the text the way Jacob's goat skins are in the text.

Defending the rods is the opposite mistake and does the Bible no favours. It is not necessary to make peeled sticks work in order to hold Scripture true; it is only necessary to read what Scripture claims. What the episode actually teaches is uncomfortable in a more useful way. Jacob spent twenty years managing a father-in-law who changed his wages ten times, and he managed him cleverly, and he prospered — and when he finally tells the story he attributes none of it to his own cleverness. Except the God of my father... had been with me, surely thou hadst sent me away now empty.
roots_summary: Hebrew luz (H3869), the hazel or almond; libneh (H3839), poplar; aqod (H6124), ringstraked; rahat (H7298), a watering trough.
roots_lines: Hebrew luz (H3869) — hazel or almond; a homonym of Luz, the old name of Bethel.
Hebrew libneh (H3839) — the white tree, poplar; named for the whiteness Jacob exposed by peeling.
Hebrew aqod (H6124) — ringstraked, banded; the marking that constituted Jacob's wages.
Hebrew rahat (H7298) — a watering trough; where the rods were set.
Hebrew patsal (H6478) — to peel, to pill; the verb of stripping the bark into white strakes.
usage: “rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree” — the materials of the scheme.
“that they should conceive when they came to drink” — the theory behind it.
“for I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee” — the real cause, given by God.

pos: n. (a small creeping animal declared unclean under the law of Moses)
etymology: Old English wesle, a weasel. In Leviticus it renders Hebrew choled, from a root meaning to glide or burrow — a creeping creature of holes and hedges, named first in the list of unclean creeping things.
biblical_def: These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind. The weasel heads a short list of small burrowing animals, and the law attached to it is not about eating but about touching: whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even. Ceremonial uncleanness was not sin and not dirt; it was a state that barred a man from the sanctuary until it was dealt with, and the whole apparatus existed to teach one lesson, stated in the same chapter: ye shall be holy; for I am holy. Israel was to be reminded at the level of the kitchen and the hedge that its God distinguishes, and that his people are distinguished. Which is why the abolition of these laws was such a violent event for a Jew. Peter, on a rooftop in Joppa, was shown a sheet of unclean creatures and told to kill and eat, and answered his Lord with a flat refusal — Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean — three times, before he understood that God had cleansed both the animals and the Gentiles standing at the gate. The weasel is a small door into a large question about what God separates and why.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a small animal of the genus Mustela, that lives in barns and about houses, and preys on mice.
webster_full: WEASEL, n. A small animal of the genus Mustela, with a long slender body, that preys on mice and birds.
UNCLEAN, a. Foul; dirty; filthy; in Jewish law, ceremonially impure and forbidden.
CREEPING, participle present. Moving on the belly, or with the body near the ground; crawling.
HOLY, a. Properly, whole, entire or perfect; hallowed; consecrated or set apart to a sacred use.
COMMON, a. In Scripture, unclean; defiled; not sanctified or set apart.
scriptures: Leviticus 11:29
These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,
Leviticus 11:31
These are unclean to you among all that creep: whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even.
Acts 10:14
But Peter said, Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.
Genesis 9:6
Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.
corruption_summary: The dietary laws are used to argue that all biblical commands are arbitrary and expired; Scripture itself abolished them, in a vision, for a stated reason, and in the same breath reasserted the holiness they had been teaching.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard argument runs that anyone who cites Leviticus on one subject must also refuse shellfish, and that the laws are therefore a matter of taste. It is a real question and Scripture answers it, not by special pleading but by its own structure. The ceremonial laws about clean and unclean creatures were expressly abolished, in a vision given to Peter, repeated three times, and interpreted in the text itself: what God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. Mark adds the Lord's own comment, that he thereby made all meats clean. The moral law was not treated that way anywhere in the New Testament; Paul goes on quoting the commandments as binding.

What should not be lost in winning that argument is what the weasel was for. Leviticus 11 ends with the reason for the whole chapter: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy. The daily business of a Hebrew household was arranged so that distinction was unavoidable — this may be touched, that may not, and the reason is the character of your God. The food laws are gone. The lesson they taught is quoted directly at the church by Peter himself: as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation.
roots_summary: Hebrew choled (H2467), a weasel or burrowing creature; tame (H2931), unclean; sherets (H8318), a swarming or creeping thing; Greek koinos (G2839), common or defiled.
roots_lines: Hebrew choled (H2467) — a weasel; from a root meaning to glide into a hole.
Hebrew tame (H2931) — ceremonially unclean; a state barring approach to the sanctuary, not a moral verdict.
Hebrew sherets (H8318) — a swarming thing; the class the weasel heads in Leviticus 11.
Hebrew qadosh (H6918) — holy, separate; the reason given for the entire chapter.
Greek koinos (G2839) — common, and so defiled; Peter's word on the rooftop, and the one God overturned.
usage: “the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise” — the head of the creeping list.
“shall be unclean until the even” — a state with a remedy and a term.
“Not so, Lord” — how hard the abolition was for the man who received it.

pos: n. (the heated quarters of a palace; where Jehoiakim burned the word of God)
etymology: A compound of winter and house, rendering Hebrew beth hachoreph — the winter apartment of a great house, distinguished from the summer house, and warmed by a brazier on the hearth.
biblical_def: Now the king sat in the winterhouse in the ninth month: and there was a fire on the hearth burning before him. Jeremiah had dictated the whole of his prophecy to Baruch, and the roll was read in the temple, then to the princes, and at last brought to Jehoiakim. The detail of the fire is given before the scene because it is the instrument. When Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed. Three or four columns at a time, cut and burned, the king warm and unhurried, working through the word of God the way a man feeds a fire. Jeremiah adds that they were not afraid, nor rent their garments — a deliberate contrast with Josiah, Jehoiakim's own father, who had rent his clothes when the book was found. Amos names the winter house in a judgment: I will smite the winter house with the summer house; and the houses of ivory shall perish. God's answer to Jehoiakim was to have the roll written again, and more added — the word he burned came back longer. Comfort is not the sin here; the winter house is only a room. What Jeremiah records is a man so settled in it that he could burn Scripture without a tremor.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a house or apartment occupied in winter; a warmed dwelling, as distinguished from a summer residence.
webster_full: WINTER-HOUSE, n. A house or apartment to be occupied in winter.
HEARTH, n. A pavement or floor of brick or stone in a chimney, on which a fire is made.
ROLL, n. A volume; a book formed of a sheet of paper or parchment rolled up.
PENKNIFE, n. A small knife used for making and mending pens.
CONSUME, v.t. To destroy by separating the parts of a thing; to burn up; to waste.
scriptures: Jeremiah 36:22
Now the king sat in the winterhouse in the ninth month: and there was a fire on the hearth burning before him.
Jeremiah 36:23

And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.
Amos 3:15
And I will smite the winter house with the summer house; and the houses of ivory shall perish, and the great houses shall have an end, saith the LORD.
Isaiah 22:9
Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many: and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool.
corruption_summary: Rejection of Scripture is imagined as a dramatic act of unbelief; Jeremiah shows it as a comfortable man with a penknife, unhurried, in a warm room, not even angry.
corruption_paragraphs: The scene is chilling precisely because it is so calm. Jehoiakim does not argue with the prophecy, does not summon scholars to refute it, does not rage. He listens to three or four leaves, cuts them off, and drops them in the fire, and repeats the procedure until the roll is gone. Jeremiah notes that the king and his servants were not afraid, nor rent their garments. Most rejection of God's word looks like this rather than like open blasphemy: a passage found unhelpful and quietly set aside, a doctrine retired as unsuited to the times, a text edited down to what the room will bear. The penknife is always small.

The answer God gave is worth as much attention as the offence. He told Jeremiah to take another roll and write all the former words again, and there were added besides unto them many like words. The word Jehoiakim burned came back longer, and it also came back with a sentence on him personally. Scripture has been burned, banned and edited in every century since and has outlasted every hearth. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
roots_summary: Hebrew choreph (H2779), winter or harvest-time; ach (H254), a fire-pan or hearth; megillah (H4039), a roll or scroll; taar (H8593), a knife or razor.
roots_lines: Hebrew choreph (H2779) — winter; the season naming the heated apartment of a palace.
Hebrew ach (H254) — a brazier or hearth; the fire burning before the king.
Hebrew megillah (H4039) — a roll, a scroll; the form in which Jeremiah's prophecies were written.
Hebrew taar (H8593) — a knife or razor; the penknife of a scribe, turned against the text.
Hebrew qara (H7167) — to rend; what Josiah did with his clothes, and what Jehoiakim did not.
usage: “the king sat in the winterhouse” — the setting given before the deed.
“he cut it with the penknife” — three or four leaves at a time.
“I will smite the winter house with the summer house” — Amos on the end of such comfort.

pos: n. (a place where flocks lie down; what God says Ammon's cities will become)
etymology: From couch, Old French coucher, from Latin collocare, to lay down, with place. It renders Hebrew mirbats, a resting or lying-down place for animals, from rabats, to crouch or lie down — the verb of Psalm 23's green pastures.
biblical_def: And I will make Rabbah a stable for camels, and the Ammonites a couchingplace for flocks: and ye shall know that I am the LORD. Rabbah was the capital of Ammon, a walled city David had besieged; the sentence is that it will become pasture. Not burned, not merely emptied — converted into the sort of ground where animals lie down at midday. Isaiah pronounces the same on Aroer: they shall be for flocks, which shall lie down, and none shall make them afraid. Zephaniah on Nineveh, the greatest city of the age: this is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me; how is she become a desolation, a place for beasts to lie down in! The judgment is quiet and complete. The Hebrew root behind couchingplace is rabats, and the same verb makes one of the most comfortable sentences in Scripture: he maketh me to lie down in green pastures. So the word cuts both ways with unsettling precision. To be a couchingplace under judgment is to be a city reduced to grass; to be made to lie down by the Shepherd is the height of safety. The difference is not in the lying down. It is in whose flock is lying there, and why the ground is quiet.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a place where cattle or flocks lie down to rest; a lair or resting place.
webster_full: COUCH, v.i. To lie down, as on a bed or place of repose; to lie down, as a beast.
COUCHING, participle present. Lying down; stooping; bending the body.
FOLD, n. A pen or inclosure for sheep; a place where a flock of sheep is kept.
DESOLATION, n. A place deserted or laid waste; ruin; destruction.
STABLE, n. A house, shed or building for beasts to lodge and feed in.
scriptures: Ezekiel 25:5
And I will make Rabbah a stable for camels, and the Ammonites a couchingplace for flocks: and ye shall know that I am the LORD.
Isaiah 17:2
The cities of Aroer are forsaken: they shall be for flocks, which shall lie down, and none shall make them afraid.
Zephaniah 2:15

This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me: how is she become a desolation, a place for beasts to lie down in! every one that passeth by her shall hiss, and wag his hand.
Zephaniah 2:6
And the sea coast shall be dwellings and cottages for shepherds, and folds for flocks.
corruption_summary: National permanence is assumed — a great city cannot simply stop — and the sentence on Ammon, Aroer and Nineveh is that the ground goes back to grass while the shepherds move in.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God ends nations, and that he does it without drama. Nineveh said in her heart I am, and there is none beside me — a phrase God uses of himself, taken up by a city — and Zephaniah's picture of the result is animals lying down in the ruins and passers-by hissing. Rabbah becomes a camel stable. The judgment is not a spectacle; it is a change of land use. Every empire that has heard this and assumed it applied to somebody else has eventually furnished the pasture.

The other half of the word is the mercy in it. Rabats, to lie down, is the verb the twenty-third Psalm uses: he maketh me to lie down in green pastures. Sheep do not lie down where they are afraid, which is why Isaiah's picture of the flocks at Aroer adds none shall make them afraid. The same God who turns a proud capital into a resting place for other men's animals is the one who gives his own people ground quiet enough to rest on. Ezekiel gives the purpose of both in the same clause: ye shall know that I am the LORD.
roots_summary: Hebrew mirbats (H4769), a place of lying down; rabats (H7257), to crouch or lie down; Rabbah (H7237), the Ammonite capital; shemamah (H8077), desolation.
roots_lines: Hebrew mirbats (H4769) — a resting place for animals; rendered couchingplace.
Hebrew rabats (H7257) — to lie down; the verb of he maketh me to lie down in green pastures.
Hebrew Rabbah (H7237) — the great city of Ammon, besieged by Joab while David stayed home.
Hebrew naveh (H5116) — a pasture or habitation; the shepherd's word for settled ground.
Hebrew shemamah (H8077) — a desolation; what Nineveh became while the flocks moved in.
usage: “the Ammonites a couchingplace for flocks” — a capital turned to pasture.
“which shall lie down, and none shall make them afraid” — the same posture, without fear.
“ye shall know that I am the LORD” — the stated purpose of the sentence.
